The Agency You Hired Spent $50K. What Did You Actually Get?

By lowob · 9 November 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · Growth / Web3 & Fintech · 5-minute read

A company can spend $50,000 on marketing, receive every promised campaign and report, and still be unable to say whether the work attracted a single valuable customer.

That's not necessarily evidence that the agency is dishonest or ineffective. It may mean the company and the agency never agreed on what success would look like. We should separate the work completed from what actually changed for the business.

First, what did the $50K actually pay for?

Imagine a small crypto exchange hiring an agency for three months. The agency launches advertisements, coordinates creator posts and delivers a monthly report. As an illustrative example, suppose $18,000 paid the agency, $24,000 was spent on advertising platforms and $8,000 paid for design and creator fees. These amounts are hypothetical, not a documented lowob client result.

$18KAgency fees

Strategy, management and reporting

$24KPaid advertising

Money spent buying ad placements

$8KProduction

Design, videos and creator fees

Each expense deserves a different question. Did the agency deliver the work it billed for? Did the advertising reach appropriate people? Did the creative explain the product? Most importantly, what was the work supposed to accomplish?

What counts as a result?

A report showing 500,000 impressions tells you ads appeared on screens about that many times. It does not mean 500,000 distinct people saw them or that anyone became a customer. A report showing website visitors is a little more useful, but it still doesn't tell you what happened after they arrived.

For a DeFi lending protocol, a meaningful result might be someone making a first deposit and remaining active after a month. For a fintech app, it could be a verified customer making a transaction. For a business selling payments infrastructure, it might be a conversation with a company that has the budget and authority to buy.

That doesn't make awareness unimportant. If you hired an agency to help potential customers understand a new category, reasonable evidence may include relevant reach, message recall, or qualified inquiries. The key is to decide on the goal together before the campaign starts.

39%

of marketing leaders in Gartner's 2025 CMO survey planned to reduce agency spending. Some cited underperforming relationships or consolidation. The survey largely covered bigger companies, not early-stage Web3 startups, but it reflects an important expectation: clients want to understand what they're getting for the money.

What two Web3 case studies actually prove

C3: Lower advertising costs, but not necessarily more traders

C3, a self-custodial exchange, worked with Web3 advertising platform Addressable to reach more relevant potential users. Instead of targeting a broad crypto audience, the campaigns focused on groups such as Avalanche traders and people interested in airdrops across different blockchains.

According to Addressable's case study, the platform then expanded those starting audiences, divided them into smaller groups and automatically adjusted which groups saw the ads based on performance. Addressable says it also provided data on trading volume and customer value to help C3 judge its advertising spending.

In the two reported campaigns, the cost of getting someone to click an ad fell from $0.71 to $0.15 and from $1.67 to $0.27. That's a substantial reduction in the price of a website visit. But the study does not publish how many additional traders those clicks produced, how valuable they were or whether they returned. Addressable is reporting the performance of its own service; the figures are not independently audited.

Green Dots: Measuring awareness and creator quality, not customer conversions

Green Dots described a $25,000 program for a blockchain ecosystem that had two related goals: create educational content and visibility for the project, while finding creators who could become reliable long-term partners. This was not primarily a campaign to acquire depositors or paying customers.

Rather than simply buying posts from creators with large followings, Green Dots reviewed more than 750 applicants, ran a three-week content challenge and selected 15 creators for a further month of paid work. Across both phases, the agency reports 190 pieces of content and approximately 967,000 views on X.

For an awareness and creator-selection campaign, the number and quality of educational posts, the audiences responding and the pool of creators ready for future work are relevant results. Green Dots also makes clear that total views are not the number of distinct people reached. Its report does not establish how many customers or dollars in revenue came from the program, nor was that the stated primary goal.

Neither case study is an independently audited evaluation. Their value here is that they illustrate different jobs an agency might be hired to do, and why the evidence should match the job.

Four questions to ask before changing agencies

What did we agree to buy?

Compare the actual contract and campaign brief with the delivered work. Was it content, awareness, new users, or qualified sales inquiries?

Where did the budget go?

Separate the agency's fees, media spend and outside costs. Ask which campaigns actually ran and what was paused or rejected.

What can we measure?

Pick a meaningful action for the business. Show the direct evidence, and explain anything the data cannot establish.

Can the current agency improve?

Clearer goals, better reporting or account access might solve the problem. A new agency won't fix an unclear assignment by itself.

Paid advertising does not always have to come last. A fixed fee is not automatically better than every other contract model. The fair test is whether the arrangement is transparent, suitable for the work, and helps both sides make better spending decisions.

The most valuable thing in an agency's report isn't a large number. It's an explanation of what happened, what remains uncertain and what the company should change next.

lowob takeaways

  • An agency can deliver what it promised without helping the business grow. Compare the work completed with the business goal, not just the number of posts or ads.
  • Know what the money bought. Separate what the agency charged from the money spent on ads, production and creators.
  • Ask what people did after seeing the marketing. A click is not automatically a funded account, an active wallet, or a qualified customer.
  • Keep access to your accounts and data. An agency can run campaigns without controlling the only copy of your reports, accounts and creative files.

Sources

Gartner: 2025 CMO Spend Survey.

Addressable: C3 case study (supplier-reported).

Green Dots: Select case study (agency-reported).
